596.title: All scripture (2 Timothy 3:14–17)
596.hook: scripture is inspired and useful for teaching and correcting (CCC 105)
596.howItsDone: Catholics hear Scripture at every Mass and many practice lectio divina, slow prayerful reading; the Church teaches that Scripture is inspired by God and is read within the living Tradition of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anazopyrein: a gift already given, fanned back into flame. Your line was fanned back into flame.

Hold your hand in front of your mouth and breathe out slowly. Warm, moving, there and then gone. Today's word is inspiration, the word the Church uses for what it teaches about the Bible. Behind it stands a single Greek word, near the end of the second letter to Timothy. Paul is reminding his young friend of the scriptures he has known since he was a child, and then he says what they are.
screen: `BREATHE ON YOUR HAND.` → `TODAY'S WORD: INSPIRATION.` → `ONE GREEK WORD IN SECOND TIMOTHY.`

segments.voice: From infancy, Paul says, you have known the holy scriptures. For Timothy, that meant the Jewish scriptures, what Christians call the Old Testament; the New was still being written. Then: "All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice, That the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work." Inspired of God is one Greek word: theopneustos. Theos, God. Pneō, to breathe. God-breathed. It may remind a reader of Genesis, where God breathes into the first man and he becomes a living soul. In that picture, the words on the page carry God's breath. Then four uses. To teach and to reprove are about what to believe. To correct and to instruct in justice are about how to live. It's a working tool, so the person of God is equipped for every good work. What do Catholics mean by inspiration? The Catechism says God is the author of Sacred Scripture. But the Second Vatican Council adds something important: the human writers were true authors too. God chose them and used them, with their own powers and abilities, their language, their style, their era. So a reader can hear Paul's temper and Luke's careful research and the psalmist's grief, and the Church still calls the words God's. The Council says the books teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wanted put into writing for the sake of our salvation. And it says Scripture must be read in the same Spirit in which it was written. For Catholics, that means reading it within the Church, together with Tradition. Breathed out once, the Church says, and breathed in every time it's read.

597.title: I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:6–8)
597.hook: Paul near the end: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course
597.carry: bring my cloak and the books
597.tomorrow: Let no man despise thy youth
597.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome pray at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, built over the place tradition names as his tomb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, inspiration: all scripture, God-breathed, through true human authors. Your line was god-breathed.

Tradition says Paul was beheaded outside the walls of Rome, near the road to Ostia, under the emperor Nero. Pilgrims still visit a great basilica built over the place tradition names as his tomb, Saint Paul Outside the Walls. In 2009, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth announced that tiny fragments of bone inside the old sarcophagus there had been dated to the first or second century. Second Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written in chains, knowing what was coming. Today, his farewell.
screen: `OUTSIDE THE WALLS OF ROME.` → `A TOMB AND A BASILICA.` → `A FAREWELL IN CHAINS.`

segments.voice: "For I am even now ready to be sacrificed: and the time of my dissolution is at hand." Ready to be sacrificed is one Greek word, spendomai: to be poured out, like wine poured over an altar as an offering. Paul sees his death that way. Not taken from him. Poured out. And the Greek word behind dissolution is analysis, a loosening: a ship slipping its moorings, soldiers striking their tents to move on. Then the sentence people carve on gravestones: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Three pictures. An athlete or a soldier who stayed in the fight. A runner who reached the line; remember Paul pressing toward the mark in Philippians. And a guard who kept what was entrusted to him, and handed it on intact. Then he looks ahead to a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will give him, and not only him, but all who love his coming. Then, right after the famous lines, something wonderfully ordinary. Bring my cloak that I left at Troas, he asks Timothy, and the books, especially the parchments. Only Luke is with me. Come before winter. A man near death, cold, a little lonely, wanting a coat and something to read. The farewell doesn't make him a statue. Catholics celebrate Paul with Peter every year on June twenty-ninth, the two apostles Rome remembers as martyrs. Kept the faith doesn't mean a spotless record. Paul never hid that he had once hunted down Christians; he called himself the least of the apostles because of it. It means he didn't put the faith down.

598.title: Let no man despise thy youth (1 Timothy 4:12)
598.hook: be an example in word, conduct, charity, faith
598.howItsDone: The Catholic Church holds World Youth Day gatherings, and Pope Francis addressed young people directly in the 2019 apostolic exhortation Christus Vivit; young saints such as Carlo Acutis are held up as examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spendomai: a life poured out, and a farewell that still asks for a cloak. Your line was bring my cloak and the books.

A meeting where nobody quite looks at the newest person when she speaks. A family dinner where the youngest one's opinion gets a pat on the head. In Ephesus, Timothy was that person. Paul had asked him to stay there and set some of the church's teachers straight. The letter never says how old he was, only that some might look down on him for being young. Paul's first letter to him has a line for exactly this.
screen: `THE YOUNGEST ONE IN THE ROOM.` → `TIMOTHY, LEFT AT EPHESUS.` → `A LINE FOR EXACTLY THIS.`

segments.voice: "Let no man despise thy youth: but be thou an example of the faithful in word, in conversation, in charity, in faith, in chastity." Look at what Paul doesn't say. He doesn't say demand respect. He doesn't say pull rank, or remind them who appointed you. He says: be an example. Earn it by how you live. Then he names five places to be seen. In word: how you speak. In conversation, which in the English of the Douay-Rheims means not talk but conduct, your whole way of life. In charity. In faith. In chastity, a clean heart. Then the habits that support it: attend to reading, to exhortation, to teaching. Meditate on these things, be wholly in them, so that your progress may be seen by all. Notice the last bit: progress. Paul doesn't expect Timothy to be finished. He expects him to be visibly growing. In the same spirit, Pope Francis wrote a whole letter to the young, called Christ Is Alive, insisting they are not only the future of the Church but its present. And the Church has canonized Carlo Acutis, an Italian teenager who loved computers and the Eucharist and died of leukemia at fifteen. Paul's advice cuts both ways. To the young, it says: be an example. To everyone else, it says the same thing as its first words. Don't despise them.

599.title: Philemon
599.hook: Paul sends a runaway slave back as a beloved brother; Christians later drew on this against slavery, too slowly
599.howItsDone: The Catholic Church today condemns slavery as an offense against human dignity (Gaudium et Spes 27; Catechism 2414), and remembers Philemon and Onesimus in its readings and saints' calendars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neotes: young Timothy, told to be an example rather than demand respect. Your line was be an example.

It's a single short chapter, written to one household, and it's about one man. His name was Onesimus, and he was enslaved in the household of a Christian named Philemon. At some point he left: whether he ran away or went looking for Paul's help, the letter doesn't say. He ended up with Paul, who was in prison, and there he became a Christian. Now Paul is sending him back, with this letter in his hand.
screen: `ONE SHORT CHAPTER, ONE MAN.` → `ONESIMUS LEAVES PHILEMON.` → `PAUL SENDS HIM BACK, WITH A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul could give orders, he says, but he'd rather ask. "I beseech thee for my son, whom I have begotten in my bands, Onesimus, Who hath been heretofore unprofitable to thee, but now is profitable both to me and thee." The name Onesimus means useful, so readers hear a pun: once useless to you, now useful. Then the heart of the letter: receive him "not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother." A brother, in the flesh and in the Lord. And Paul puts his own name on the line: if he owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write it with my own hand. I will repay it. Now the hard part, said plainly. Paul never commands Philemon to set Onesimus free. He says he's confident Philemon will do even more than he asks, and readers have argued ever since about whether that's a hint. Nobody knows what Philemon did. And this little letter was later used on both sides. Some slaveholders, including in the American South, cited it to defend returning people who had escaped. Others pointed to its words, no longer a servant but a brother, against slavery itself. Christians, the Catholic Church among them, came to condemn slavery too slowly. Popes condemned the slave trade in the nineteenth century, and the Second Vatican Council listed slavery among the things that poison human society and insult the Creator. Some years later, Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church at Ephesus, named its bishop Onesimus. Some think it was the same man. Nobody can be sure.

600.title: Sharper than a sword (Hebrews 4:12)
600.hook: the word of God is living and effectual
600.howItsDone: At Mass the Book of the Gospels may be carried in the entrance procession, placed on the altar, incensed and kissed before the Gospel is proclaimed; Catholics stand to hear the Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philemon: Onesimus sent back not as a servant but as a most dear brother. Your line was no longer a servant.

The letter to the Hebrews names no author. The Douay-Rheims heads it as Paul's, and the Church long counted it among his letters, but early Christians also suggested Barnabas, or Luke, or Clement of Rome. Origen, the scholar of Alexandria, said, more or less, that only God knows who wrote it down. It reads less like a letter than a sermon, for Christians who were tired and tempted to drift away. Hebrews and James start today, and this preacher has a lot to say about how God speaks.
screen: `NO NAME ON THE LETTER.` → `ONLY GOD KNOWS WHO WROTE IT DOWN.` → `A SERMON FOR THE TIRED.`

segments.voice: He's just been quoting a psalm: today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts. Today. The psalm was centuries old, and he treats it as spoken right now, to his listeners. Then today's verse: "For the word of God is living and effectual, and more piercing than any two edged sword; and reaching unto the division of the soul and the spirit, of the joints also and the marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." Living: not a fossil. Effectual is the Greek energes: active, at work. It does things. Then the sword. Look at what it cuts: soul from spirit, joints from marrow. Some readers hear surgery here more than battle, a scalpel more than a weapon, reaching places you can't reach yourself and showing what's actually there. Discerner, in Greek, is kritikos: one able to judge. In Hebrews' picture, the word of God reads you while you read it. The next verse says it plainly: nothing is hidden from his sight, everything is naked and open to his eyes. That could sound frightening. Read another way, it's the start of healing: you can't treat what you can't see. Catholics honor the word with their bodies. At Mass the Book of the Gospels can be carried in procession, held high, incensed and kissed. The Second Vatican Council said the Church has always venerated the Scriptures just as it venerates the Lord's body, and that in them the Father meets his children and speaks with them.

601.title: One who has compassion (Hebrews 4:14–16)
601.hook: a high priest tempted in all things like us, without sin
601.tomorrow: The substance of things hoped for
601.howItsDone: Catholics bring their weaknesses to Christ in personal prayer, in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament, and in the sacrament of penance, where they believe Christ forgives through the priest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kritikos: the word of God, living and effectual, reading you while you read it. Your line was living and effectual.

Before an operation, a nurse who once had the same surgery can say the same words as one who hasn't: it'll be okay. They land differently, because she's been there. Hebrews builds much of its argument around a picture from Israel's worship: the high priest, who once a year, on the Day of Atonement, entered the holiest place to seek mercy for the people. Today the preacher says something surprising about the high priest Christians have.
screen: `A NURSE WHO'S BEEN THERE.` → `THE HIGH PRIEST, ONCE A YEAR.` → `A HIGH PRIEST WHO UNDERSTANDS.`

segments.voice: First, who it is: a great high priest who has passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, so hold fast to what you profess. Then the surprise: "For we have not a high priest, who can not have compassion on our infirmities: but one tempted in all things like as we are, without sin." The Greek verb for have compassion is sympathēsai: to suffer with, to feel alongside. Not pity from above; fellow feeling from inside. Hebrews means it. A chapter later it says that in the days of his flesh he offered prayers and supplications with a strong cry and tears. The Gospels show him hungry in the desert, tempted there, exhausted, grieving at a friend's tomb, in anguish in Gethsemane. And yet without sin. Catholic teaching holds both together: the Council of Chalcedon said he is like us in all things but sin. In this picture, sinlessness doesn't make him distant from the tempted. Some Christian writers have argued that one who never gave way under temptation felt its full weight, and so knows its full strength. Then the invitation: "Let us go therefore with confidence to the throne of grace: that we may obtain mercy, and find grace in seasonable aid." The Greek word for confidence means boldness, the freedom to speak openly. Seasonable aid means help at the right moment, when you need it. Catholics hear this invitation in personal prayer, before the tabernacle, and in confession, where they believe Christ's mercy meets them through the priest.

602.title: The substance of things hoped for (Hebrews 11)
602.hook: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sara and the long list of the faithful
602.howItsDone: Catholics hear parts of Hebrews 11 in the Sunday and weekday readings at Mass, and the chapter's list of the faithful is often read alongside the Church's teaching on the communion of saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sympathēsai: a high priest tempted in all things like us, without sin. Your line was he understands.

Names written inside the cover of an old Bible. Photos stuck to a fridge. A grandmother who prayed through a war. An uncle who started over in a new country with one suitcase. Many families keep a list like this somewhere. Nobody on it is perfect, and all of them kept walking toward something they couldn't see yet. Hebrews eleven is that list for the whole Church. After ten chapters on Christ the high priest, and before the hard advice of chapter twelve, the writer stops and reads out the family names. He opens with a definition.
screen: `NAMES INSIDE AN OLD BIBLE.` → `HEBREWS READS THE FAMILY LIST.` → `IT OPENS WITH A DEFINITION.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "Now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not." Substance first. The Greek word is hypostasis, literally what stands underneath: a foundation, the thing that holds something up. In this line faith isn't a mood or a guess. It's the ground under a hope, giving it somewhere to stand before it arrives. Then evidence: a conviction about what can't be seen yet. Then the names, each opening the same way: by faith. By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain. Noah built an ark for a flood nobody had ever seen. Abraham "went out, not knowing whither he went." Sara, long past the age for children, received strength to conceive, because she believed that the one who promised was faithful. Then Moses, Rahab, and a rush of names the writer says there isn't time to finish: Gideon, Samson, David, Samuel, the prophets. Here's the surprise. The chapter says plainly that these people died without receiving what was promised. They saw it from far off and greeted it, like travelers waving at a city on the horizon. And the last verse says they would not be made perfect without us. The list isn't closed; it's waiting for more names. Catholics hear the communion of saints in this: the faithful who have gone before are still one family with the living. The next chapter calls them a cloud of witnesses, surrounding the race.
screen: `HYPOSTASIS: WHAT STANDS UNDERNEATH.` · `BY FAITH: ABEL, NOAH, ABRAHAM, SARA.` · `THEY DIED WITHOUT RECEIVING IT.` · `NOT MADE PERFECT WITHOUT US.` · then, large: `FAITH IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS TO BE HOPED FOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose faith held you up, alive or gone: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who kept going through something hard. Say their name quietly, then finish the line the way Hebrews does, by faith, they..., and let it end however it ends: kept a promise, got up early to pray, forgave. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if not, hold the name with gratitude.
Faith. In Hebrews eleven, the substance of things hoped for: the ground a hope stands on before it arrives. Today's word.
Your line: faith is the substance. And that's week eighty-six: god-breathed, spendomai, be an example, Philemon, kritikos, he understands, and faith. Day six hundred two, done.
